strengths: The paper is technically careful and largely self-contained: the spectral analysis of the simplex FIM (Theorem 1, Lemmas 2-5) is derived rigorously using classical tools (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin discs, Hoffman-Wielandt, Von Neumann trace inequality), with complete proofs in the appendix.

The Hutchinson-style FIM estimator is a genuinely useful construction: it is unbiased, requires only one additional backward pass, is architecture-agnostic, works for the full tensor, diagonal, or block-diagonal cases, and comes with explicit variance guarantees (CV bounded by sqrt(2) for diagonal entries, Prop. 12-14).

The paper clearly identifies and quantifies the bias and worst-case error of the widely used empirical Fisher (Lemmas 4-5, Props. 10-11), including the nice adversarial-label argument, which is of independent pedagogical value.

The framework connecting the low-dimensional 'core space' metric to the neuromanifold FIM via the pullback/Gauss-Newton structure (Eq. 4) is cleanly exploited to transfer core-space bounds to the network setting.
Related work is well positioned, with a fair comparison to Monte Carlo estimators, Kronecker-factored approximations, and recent work on diagonal Fisher estimator trade-offs (Soen & Sun 2024).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core theoretical results: the simplex FIM is diag(p) - pp^T, whose spectrum (zero eigenvalue along e, sum of eigenvalues, interlacing with diag(p)) is largely classical. Theorem 1 is a modest refinement of well-known facts about rank-1 perturbations of diagonal matrices.

The Hutchinson estimator idea is fairly incremental: applying Hutchinson/Gaussian probes to estimate outer-product-based expectations is standard, and the sqrt(p(y|x)) * xi_y construction is a straightforward application of the identity F = E_p[(grad l)(grad l)^T]. The main advantage (all C label-gradients in one backward pass) is an efficiency gain rather than a conceptual advance, and the paper does not thoroughly distinguish it from prior sampling-based Fisher estimators.

Evaluation is very weak for a top-tier venue: the only experiments are kernel-density plots of diagonal FIM entries of DistilBERT on AG News and SST-2 using 128 samples. There is no quantitative error measurement against a ground-truth FIM (e.g., on small models where exact computation is possible), no ablation on the number of Hutchinson samples or power-iteration steps, and no demonstration of downstream utility (optimization, natural gradient, regularization) where the estimator's guarantees would matter.

The practical value of the deterministic Loewner-order bounds (Prop. 6, 8, 9) is not demonstrated: the rank-1 lower bound requires eigenvector computation via power iteration per sample, and the paper itself notes it is 'relatively expensive'; no experiment shows these bounds are tighter or more useful than the unbiased estimator in practice.

The claimed advantage over MC estimators (unbounded CV for MC vs. bounded CV for Hutchinson) rests on a stylized single-neuron example with heavy-tailed inputs; a more general or empirical comparison of estimator quality would strengthen the central claim.

Several presentation issues: heavy notation with multiple nearly identical symbols (F-hat used for both eFIM and MC-FIM, acknowledged as an 'abuse of notation'), minor typos ('It is know', 'estiamte', 'latter'/'later'), and Lemma 3's characterization of diag(p) as incurring error at least 1/C is presented without discussion of its practical significance.

The abstract's claim of an unbiased estimate with 'standard deviation bounded by the true value up to scaling' holds for diagonal entries only in the presented analysis; extension to the full tensor is asserted but not developed.

strengths: The paper is technically careful: the linear algebra (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin discs, Von Neumann trace inequality, Hoffman-Wielandt) is applied correctly, and the proofs in the appendices are complete and self-contained.

The proposed Hutchinson-style estimator F(θ) is a clean, unbiased, architecture-agnostic estimator of the FIM computable with a single extra backward pass, which is a practically relevant observation.

The deterministic Löwner-order bounds (Propositions 6-9) with quantifiable error terms, and the analysis of when the lower bound is tighter than the upper bound, are somewhat interesting results on the core simplex space.
The writing is generally clear, with useful notation tables and honest positioning of the estimators' variance guarantees (bounded CV via Cantelli inequality).
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea — applying Hutchinson's trick to obtain an unbiased FIM estimate via a scalar random loss function — is a fairly direct adaptation of a well-known technique (already used for Hessian traces, Gaussian process FIMs, and diagonal Fisher estimates, as the authors themselves acknowledge in Section 5). The deterministic bounds are competent but standard applications of classical spectral results. The paper reads more as a well-executed exercise than a conceptual advance.

Very weak empirical evaluation. The only experiments are kernel-density plots of diagonal FIM entries on DistilBERT (AG News and SST-2) with 128 samples. There is no downstream task demonstrating the estimators' utility (e.g., natural gradient optimization, uncertainty estimation, model pruning, or trace-based regularizers), no empirical comparison of accuracy/variance trade-offs against MC-FIM or the estimators of Soen & Sun [30], no runtime benchmarks despite efficiency being a central claimed advantage, and no validation that the bounds are tight on realistic models beyond eyeballing density plots.

The practical significance of the contributions is not established. The paper admits in the conclusion that applications such as new optimizers are 'not developed here and left as meaningful future work.' For a top-tier venue, a methods paper whose estimators are claimed to be 'practical for large scale networks' should demonstrate at least one convincing use case where the guaranteed-quality estimate matters.

Some results are underwhelming in scope. Lemma 2's bounds are exact restatements of the spectral decomposition; several propositions (e.g., Corollary 7, Propositions 8-11) provide bounds whose tightness on realistic neural networks is never assessed quantitatively. The claim that the analysis 'improves existing bounds' over [30] is asserted without a comparative experiment or even a formal comparison.

Presentation issues further weaken the paper: notation is heavy (multiple tensor superscripts DG/LR/∆/C plus hat conventions that are overloaded across estimators, acknowledged in Table 1), the proof of Theorem 1 duplicates the interlacing bound it just derived ('which has just been proved'), and there are typographical problems ('show latter', 'It is know', 'estiamte').

The motivation for the deterministic bounds is unclear in practice: computing the lower bound requires power iteration to estimate λC and vC per sample, yet no experiment quantifies this cost or the accuracy of the resulting bound, so it is hard to judge whether the 'guaranteed quality' framework has practical value over simply running the unbiased estimator.

strengths: Technically solid mathematical development: the paper provides complete, self-contained proofs for its spectral analysis of the simplex FIM (Theorem 1), deterministic Löwner-order bounds (Lemmas 2-3, Propositions 6-11), and variance guarantees for the proposed Hutchinson-style estimators (Propositions 12-14), with detailed proofs in the appendix.

The proposed Hutchinson-based FIM estimator is elegant and practical: it is architecture-agnostic, unbiased, computable with a single extra backward pass via auto-differentiation interfaces (e.g., Tensor.detach()), and comes with a concrete quality guarantee (CV bounded by sqrt(2)), which is a genuine improvement over the unbounded CV of the MC estimator shown in Section 4.1.
The analysis of the eFIM's adversarial bias (Lemmas 4-5, Proposition 11) is a useful, interpretable contribution that formalizes well-known practical concerns about empirical Fisher approximations.
The paper is clearly written with careful notation, honest positioning in related work, and correct derivations overall.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components. The simplex FIM diag(p) - pp^T and its spectrum are classical; the eigenvalue bounds follow from standard tools (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin discs, Von Neumann trace inequality). The core estimator is a direct application of Hutchinson's trick to the class dimension of the FIM, and Hutchinson-based FIM/Hessian trace estimation already exists (refs [9, 11, 31]); the paper's contribution is largely a careful synthesis rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The empirical evaluation is very weak and does not support the central claims. It consists only of kernel density plots of diagonal FIM entries on a single model (DistilBERT) with 128 samples. There is no quantitative validation of the proposed bounds (e.g., tightness of Theorem 1 or Propositions 8-9 is asserted from 'numerical simulations' but never shown), no comparison against ground-truth FIM or alternative estimators (K-FAC, EKFAC, MC FIM with multiple samples, Soen & Sun 2024), and no error/variance measurements against the theoretical guarantees.

No demonstration of practical utility. The motivating applications (natural gradient, regularizers) are never exercised: no optimizer, no downstream task improvement, no runtime benchmark against competing estimators. The conclusion explicitly defers all real applications to future work, which significantly weakens the significance claim.

The rank-1-per-sample nature of the estimator, variance accumulation across training steps, and the effect of using more Hutchinson samples are discussed only in passing; ablations on number of samples, dataset size, and architectures are missing.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the experiments are small-scale enough that claims about scalability to 'large scale networks' remain untested.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., the claim that the bounds 'improve over existing bounds' (e.g., [30]) is made without any empirical or quantitative head-to-head comparison.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: the theoretical results (spectrum of the simplex FIM, Löwner-order envelopes, deterministic bounds on the neuromanifold FIM, and unbiasedness/variance bounds for the Hutchinson estimators) are stated precisely and complete proofs are provided in the appendix.

The proposed Hutchinson-based FIM estimator is practically attractive: it is unbiased, has provably bounded coefficient of variation (≤ √2 per diagonal entry), and can be implemented with a single extra backward pass, making it scalable to large models.

The empirical study covers a diverse set of production-scale models and modalities (DistilBERT/RobERTa on NLP, ResNet-50/EfficientNet-B0 on vision, Wav2Vec2 on speech), with ground-truth diagonal FIM computed in closed form for comparison, which is a nontrivial evaluation effort.
The analysis of limitations of MC and empirical FIM estimators (unbounded coefficient of variation for heavy-tailed inputs, adversarially bad eFIM errors) is informative and well-motivated.
The paper is well written and clearly structured, with careful notation and honest positioning of limitations (e.g., the rank-1 nature of the estimate, the singular metric issue in footnotes).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core idea. The Fisher information of the categorical/simplex model, I(z) = diag(p) - ppᵀ, is a classical result, and the spectral analysis (kernel direction e, interlacing, Gershgorin bounds) follows from standard tools. The Hutchinson estimator is a fairly direct application of Hutchinson's trick to log-likelihood gradients; closely related Hutchinson-based Hessian/FIM trace estimators and the diagonal Fisher estimator trade-off analysis (Soen & Sun, NeurIPS 2024, cited by the authors) already exist, making the delta over prior work incremental.

The evaluation is largely descriptive. There is no downstream application demonstrating that the improved estimator quality actually matters: no natural gradient/optimizer, pruning, fine-tuning, or curvature-based experiments. The paper itself admits the results 'are not directly piped into a downstream application,' which significantly weakens the significance claim.

The practical advantage over the empirical FIM is thin in the experiments: both require one backward pass per batch, speedup factors are ~0.88–1.07 (often slower), and the proposed estimator wins on relative error only in some settings, while the biased low-rank estimates 𝒫^LR are best on fine-tuned tasks. The claimed advantage of unbiasedness is not connected to measurable consequences.

The experiments use only 128 batches of size 64 and a single run per setting; no variance/confidence estimates across data subsets or probe samples are reported, despite variance being a central theoretical topic of the paper.

Some results are weak or loose in practice: the deterministic bounds depend on quantities (singular values of ∂z/∂θ, order statistics of p) that are not characterized for realistic networks, so the bounds' usefulness on real neuromanifolds is unclear; Proposition 9's bound is acknowledged by the authors to be loose.

The low-rank and diagonal-core estimators (ℎ^LR, ℎ^DG) require power iterations or spectral decompositions of the C×C core per sample, and lose substantially in speed for moderate/large C, limiting their applicability relative to the main 𝒫 estimator.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code release is mentioned, and implementation details for the ground-truth FIM computation (1892C backward passes) and the fixed power-iteration budget are given only at a high level.

strengths: The paper is technically careful and self-contained: the pullback structure of the FIM through the simplex core is clearly articulated, and the deterministic bounds (Propositions 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) are derived rigorously with complete proofs in the appendix.

The proposed Hutchinson-based estimator I(F)(theta) is attractive from a systems standpoint: it is an unbiased estimate of the full FIM (including diagonal entries and trace) computable with a single extra backward pass per batch, requires no Hessian-vector products, and is architecture-agnostic. Proven variance bounds (CV <= sqrt(2)) are a genuine guarantee that the plain Monte Carlo estimator lacks.

The analysis of the failure modes of the empirical FIM (Propositions 9-10) and of the unbounded coefficient of variation of MC estimates (Section 4.1) is a useful cautionary contribution that is clearly explained.

Experiments cover a reasonable diversity of modalities (NLP, vision, speech) and model families, and the evaluation against ground-truth diagonal FIM entries (via a closed-form but expensive computation) is methodologically sound, using an interpretable error metric (RelMAE).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core-space theory. Theorem 1 (spectrum of the simplex FIM diag(p) - pp^T, kernel spanned by e, eigenvalue sum 1 - ||p||^2) and Lemma 2 (best rank-1 and best diagonal envelopes) are essentially textbook linear algebra of rank-one perturbations of diagonal matrices, obtained via Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin discs, and Von Neumann's trace inequality. The downstream network-level bounds follow mechanically by pulling these back through the Jacobian, so the theoretical contribution feels incremental.

Limited novelty of the estimator. Hutchinson's trick applied to Fisher information traces is already established (e.g., Jastrzebski et al., 2021; Stein et al., 2013), and the proposed estimator is a natural variance-reduced variant of the standard rank-one Monte Carlo estimator with a shared probe vector. The paper's own related-work section concedes that MC-estimator accuracy has been analyzed before (Guo & Spall, 2019; Soen & Sun, 2021, 2024); the delta over this line of work is not sharply quantified.

The evaluation does not demonstrate downstream utility. The conclusion explicitly admits the estimator is not piped into any application (no optimizer, pruning, fine-tuning, or regularization experiment uses I(F)). For a paper whose motivation rests on the importance of accurate FIM estimates for natural gradient, pruning, and forgetting, showing improved end-task behavior is a significant missing piece.

Evaluation is confined to the diagonal FIM on a single fixed subset of 128 batches of size 64. Off-diagonal structure, full-matrix quality, sensitivity to probe distribution (Gaussian vs. Rademacher), and the effect of the number of probes J are not empirically characterized, even though the theory suggests these matter.

The empirical results are mixed and somewhat undercut the headline recommendation: the proposed estimator I(F) is best on only some tasks, while the deterministic low-rank estimators I(F^LR) win on fine-tuned models (SST-2, MNLI), and I(F^DG) is worst on two of six tasks. The practical guidance ('choose I(F) by default') is weaker than the framing suggests.

Significance concerns: the bounds in Propositions 7-9 are acknowledged by the authors to be loose, and the tightest estimator (low-rank core) is the most expensive, requiring spectral decomposition or power iteration per sample. The practical niche of each method remains unclear.
No released code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned despite the implementation details (detach() tricks, power-iteration budget T=30) being central to the practical claims.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: the core-space analysis (Theorem 1, Lemmas 2-4) is clean and the proofs (appendices E-R) are careful, using standard but appropriate tools (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin discs, Von Neumann trace inequality, Hoffman-Wielandt).

The deterministic bounds (Propositions 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) are novel in being built on envelopes in the core space and on order statistics of the output probability vector, and the tightness/error analysis of each bound is a genuine contribution over prior theoretical bounds (e.g., Soen & Sun 2021/2024).

The proposed Hutchinson-style estimator F is a nice, practical contribution: it is unbiased with provably bounded CV (Proposition 11), computable via a single extra backward pass with a detach() trick, architecture-agnostic, and directly implementable in autodiff frameworks; the variant estimators for diagonal and low-rank cores (Section 4.3-4.4, Props 13-14) round out a coherent family.
The illustration that MC FIM can have unbounded coefficient of variation (Section 4.1) is a clear, well-motivated argument for why the new estimator is preferable.

Evaluation covers a reasonably diverse set of models and modalities (DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, Wav2Vec2) with ground-truth diagonal FIM comparison, an interpretable error metric (RelMAE), and honest discussion of when baselines win (fine-tuned low-rank regimes).
Writing is generally clear, notation is carefully laid out, and limitations are candidly stated (diagonal-only analysis, no downstream application yet).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than striking: Hutchinson's trick is long-established for trace/Hessian estimation, and applying it to the FIM by randomly flipping the log-likelihood with a Rademacher/Gaussian probe is a fairly direct adaptation; the closest related work (Soen & Sun 2024 on trade-offs of diagonal FIM estimators) makes the delta appear incremental in places.
The headline theoretical result on the core space (Theorem 1, spectrum of diag(p)-pp^T) is elementary and likely folklore-adjacent; its contribution is in packaging rather than depth.

Empirical evaluation is narrow: only the diagonal FIM is compared, on a single fixed subset of 128 batches of size 64; there is no demonstration on any downstream task (optimization, pruning, forgetting, trace regularizers), and the authors themselves concede the estimator is 'not directly piped into a downstream application', which weakens the significance claim.

Some bounds are admittedly loose (Propositions 7, 9), and the low-rank core estimator requires spectral decomposition or power iteration per sample, incurring roughly half the speed (or worse, e.g., 0.46x-0.51x on CIFAR-100), which limits its practical appeal.
The ground truth is only approximate (closed-form diagonal FIM on a small subset), so accuracy claims rest on a proxy; statistical variability across subsets/seeds is not reported.
Several design details (fixed T=30 power iterations, single probe per batch, accumulated averaging along the trajectory) are justified only heuristically rather than ablated.
